Attributes, aliases and conversion

Source: vignettes/attributes.Rmd
attributes.Rmd

Motivation

Figures about people are collected for places, and every table describes the places at its own resolution: one lists cities, another regions, a third whole countries. The numbers that turn one quantity into another – the persons that make a household, the litres of water a person uses in a day – are published in the same uneven way: for some places, and often at a resolution other than the one the data is recorded at.

A nested scale keeps such numbers as attributes: values that belong to a member at whatever frame they are published, resolved down the hierarchy when a finer member has none of its own, and applied row by row. The same mechanism serves any dimension – a wage per industry, an hour count per time slice. This vignette works on people in cities.

An example scale

Eight cities in four regions in two countries. All names and all numbers in this vignette are invented round values, chosen for illustration; none is a statistic. Two attributes are attached under the source "census": the persons per household (hh_size, in persons/household) for six cities, and the water use per person and day (water_use, in litres/person) for four.

values <- data.frame(
  frame = "city",
  member = c("Alder", "Birch", "Cedar", "Elm", "Fern", "Grove",
             "Alder", "Cedar", "Elm", "Grove"),
  attribute = rep(c("hh_size", "water_use"), c(6, 4)),
  kind = rep(c("property", "factor"), c(6, 4)),
  value = c(2, 3, 2.5, 2, 2.5, 3.5, 150, 120, 100, 200),
  unit_of_measure = rep(c("persons/household", "litres/person"), c(6, 4)),
  source = "census"
)
codes <- data.frame(
  frame = c("city", "city", "region", "country"),
  member = c("Alder", "Grove", "Harbour", "North"),
  alias = c("ALD", "GRV", "HBR", "NTH"),
  source = "short"
)
places <- scale_from_leaftable(
  data.frame(
    country = c("North", "North", "North", "North",
                "South", "South", "South", "South"),
    region = c("N1", "N1", "N2", "N2", "S1", "S1", "S1", "Harbour"),
    city = c("Alder", "Birch", "Cedar", "Dale", "Elm", "Fern", "Grove",
             "Harbour")
  ),
  frames = c("country", "region", "city"), name = "places",
  attributes = values, aliases = codes
)
places
#> NestedScale: places
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - country (2)
#>     - region (4)
#>       - city (8)
#> Leaves: 8
#> Attributes: hh_size, water_use (sources: census) -- 10 at city
#> Aliases: 4 (short)
scale_members(places, "region")
#> [1] "N1"      "N2"      "S1"      "Harbour"
scale_children(places, "region", "S1")
#> [1] "Elm"   "Fern"  "Grove"

Codes repeat across frames (Harbour is a region and the only city inside it), so every lookup names its frame.

Where a city has no value, there is no number – the package never fills one in:

hh_size <- scale_attributes(places, "hh_size", frame = "city")
hh_size[c("member", "value", "unit_of_measure", "source")]
#>    member value   unit_of_measure source
#> 1   Alder   2.0 persons/household census
#> 2   Birch   3.0 persons/household census
#> 3   Cedar   2.5 persons/household census
#> 4    Dale    NA              <NA>   <NA>
#> 5     Elm   2.0 persons/household census
#> 6    Fern   2.5 persons/household census
#> 7   Grove   3.5 persons/household census
#> 8 Harbour    NA              <NA>   <NA>

Attributes are not weights

A weight says how big a leaf is: the hours in a time slice, the area of a region, the people of a city. Weights drive aggregation (weighted_mean up) and disaggregation (sum split down). They are declared on the leaftable and sum over the scale.

A household size is none of those things. It is a conversion factor: it turns the households of this city into persons, row by row, and summing it over cities is meaningless. A scale therefore keeps attributes in a separate table, keyed by (frame, member), and consumes them only in convert_scale(). The constructor promotes numeric leaftable columns to weights; a household size passed as a column would become a weight and be summed. It is passed as attributes= instead.

Averaging an attribute over several members is a legitimate aggregation – the mean household size of a region, given how many households each of its cities has. That is an ordinary recast of a resolved attribute with the weighted_mean rule, and the weight is where weights live: on the scale, as the number of households of each city.

s1 <- filter_scale(places, "region", "S1")
lt <- scale_leaftable(s1)
lt$households <- c(3000, 400, 2000)
south1 <- scale_from_leaftable(
  lt, frames = c("country", "region", "city"),
  attributes = scale_attributes(s1), name = "south1"
)
hh_s1 <- scale_attributes(south1, "hh_size", frame = "city")
recast_scale(
  data.frame(city = hh_s1$member, hh_size = hh_s1$value), south1,
  source = "city", target = "region", rule = "weighted_mean",
  weight = "households"
)
#>   region  hh_size
#> 1     S1 2.592593

(filter_scale() keeps only the attribute rows of the surviving members, so the subset’s table is exactly what the new scale may take.)

Attributes live at any frame, and resolve by nearest ancestor

A value may be stored on a city, on a region or on a country. When a city has no value of its own, scale_attributes() walks to the nearest coarser frame that holds one and reports where the value came from. The census values are all at the city frame; a region-wide figure from another source fills the gaps below it without touching the cities that have their own:

regional <- attach_attributes_scale(
  places,
  data.frame(frame = "region", member = "N2", attribute = "hh_size",
             kind = "property", value = 3,
             unit_of_measure = "persons/household"),
  source = "regional"
)
res <- scale_attributes(regional, "hh_size", frame = "city")
res[res$member %in% scale_children(regional, "region", "N2"),
    c("member", "value", "source", "origin_frame", "origin_member")]
#>   member value   source origin_frame origin_member
#> 3  Cedar   2.5   census         city         Cedar
#> 4   Dale   3.0 regional       region            N2

Cedar keeps its own value; Dale inherits the region’s. Nothing is guessed from a neighbouring city or an average.

Two situations are refused rather than resolved:

  • Ambiguity across a cross-cutting frame. When the walk reaches a frame where the member has several ancestors and one of them holds the attribute, it cannot pick one and errors; if none does, it continues to the next coarser frame. vignette("anatomy") builds a scale with such a frame.
  • Several sources. Two sources publishing the same attribute for the same member is an error unless source= chooses. The walk stays within the chosen source: a source that lacks a city reports NA rather than borrowing another’s figure.

In the chunk below a survey reports its own household size for Alder, which the census already covers. The first read fails for that reason; the second names the source.

two <- attach_attributes_scale(
  places,
  data.frame(frame = "city", member = "Alder", attribute = "hh_size",
             kind = "property", value = 2.2,
             unit_of_measure = "persons/household"),
  source = "survey"
)
scale_attributes(two, "hh_size", frame = "city")
#> Error:
#> ! `hh_size` for `Alder` at frame `city` is published by several sources (census, survey); pass `source=`
survey <- scale_attributes(two, "hh_size", frame = "city", source = "survey")
survey[!is.na(survey$value), c("member", "value", "source")]
#>   member value source
#> 1  Alder   2.2 survey

Sources and provenance

Every attribute row names its source and unit_of_measure. Attaching never overwrites: a row with the same (frame, member, attribute, source) is an error, so a better number is added by attaching it under its own source name and selecting it. Every attribute name carries a kind (SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS): a property is an invertible ratio, a factor converts one way only. Any attribute name is accepted.

People to households, with the household size

convert_scale() applies to each row the attribute resolved for its city. hh_size is stored in persons/household, so it multiplies households into persons and, being a property, divides persons into households. The two units are matched as plain strings, exactly as they are written in unit_of_measure. The result reports which value was applied and where it came from.

pop <- data.frame(
  city     = c("Alder", "Cedar", "Elm", "Grove"),
  people_k = c(3, 5, 6, 7)
)
# thousands -> persons: no prefix arithmetic is done
pop$persons <- pop$people_k * 1e3
hh <- convert_scale(pop[c("city", "persons")], places, "hh_size",
                    from_unit = "persons", to_unit = "household")
names(hh)[names(hh) == "persons"] <- "households"
hh
#>    city households hh_size hh_size.origin_frame
#> 1 Alder       1500     2.0                 city
#> 2 Cedar       2000     2.5                 city
#> 3   Elm       3000     2.0                 city
#> 4 Grove       2000     3.5                 city

A property converts both ways, so the households return the persons:

convert_scale(hh[c("city", "households")], places, "hh_size",
              from_unit = "household", to_unit = "persons")
#>    city households hh_size hh_size.origin_frame
#> 1 Alder       3000     2.0                 city
#> 2 Cedar       5000     2.5                 city
#> 3   Elm       6000     2.0                 city
#> 4 Grove       7000     3.5                 city

A city without a value

A city without a value is an error, not a silent zero. Dale has no household size in the census, so a table that includes it is refused:

more <- data.frame(city = c("Cedar", "Dale"), persons = c(5000, 4000))
convert_scale(more, places, "hh_size",
              from_unit = "persons", to_unit = "household")
#> Error:
#> ! no `hh_size` value resolves for Dale at frame `city`; attach one with attach_attributes_scale() or pass na_action = "keep"

na_action = "keep" converts the rows that have a value and carries NA in the others:

convert_scale(more, places, "hh_size",
              from_unit = "persons", to_unit = "household",
              na_action = "keep")
#>    city persons hh_size hh_size.origin_frame
#> 1 Cedar    2000     2.5                 city
#> 2  Dale      NA      NA                 <NA>

Aggregate to regions

Aggregation is a recast with an explicit rule; sum conserves the total. The rule is registered once per column, or passed as rule= each time.

One decision has to be stated. The table reports four cities against a scale of eight. By default an absent city is unknown, and every region that contains one aggregates to NA with a warning – the safe reading for incomplete data. Here the table is meant as the complete list of what is to be counted, the households of the four cities and no others, and missing_sources = "ignore" says so. The regional figures are then totals of the reported cities, not estimates for the whole regions. The warning still names the absent cities, and a region with no reported city at all, Harbour, has no total.

households <- hh[c("city", "households")]
register_scale_rule("households", "sum")
by_region <- recast_scale(households, places, source = "city",
                          target = "region", missing_sources = "ignore")
#> Warning: 4 source member(s) present in the scale but missing from the data
#> (e.g. Birch, Dale, Fern, ... (4 total)); produced NAs
by_region
#>    region households
#> 1      N1       1500
#> 2      N2       2000
#> 3      S1       5000
#> 4 Harbour         NA
sum(by_region$households, na.rm = TRUE) == sum(households$households)
#> [1] TRUE

Water use, one-way

A water use per person converts persons to litres and nothing else: the litres drawn in a city say nothing certain about how many people live there. water_use is therefore stored with kind factor, not property, and convert_scale() refuses the inverse.

water <- convert_scale(pop[c("city", "persons")], places, "water_use",
                       from_unit = "person", to_unit = "litres")
names(water)[names(water) == "persons"] <- "litres"
water
#>    city  litres water_use water_use.origin_frame
#> 1 Alder  450000       150                   city
#> 2 Cedar  600000       120                   city
#> 3   Elm  600000       100                   city
#> 4 Grove 1400000       200                   city
convert_scale(water[c("city", "litres")], places, "water_use",
              from_unit = "litres", to_unit = "person")
#> Error:
#> ! `water_use` converts person -> litres only; the inverse is refused because it is a factor, not a property (see SCALE_ATTRIBUTE_KINDS)

Values from a published source

Reference values – the tables of a census, the results of a household survey, the register of a single municipality – are attached the same way: a table with one row per member and attribute, under the name of its source. Each source is chosen with source= when reading; nothing is overwritten.

own <- attach_attributes_scale(
  places,
  data.frame(frame = "city", member = "Grove", attribute = "hh_size",
             kind = "property", value = 3.4,
             unit_of_measure = "persons/household"),
  source = "register"
)
register <- scale_attributes(own, "hh_size", frame = "city",
                             source = "register")
register[!is.na(register$value), c("member", "value", "source")]
#>   member value   source
#> 7  Grove   3.4 register

Names and short codes

Tables name places in different ways: one by the official name, another by a short code. scale_match() resolves both through the alias table, exactly and case-insensitively, first against member names and then against aliases, and reports ambiguity instead of guessing. There is no fuzzy or substring stage: a near miss is reported as unmatched, not repaired.

scale_match(places, c("ALD", "grove", "HBR", "Harbour", "Zed"))
#>     label  frame  member    method                   candidates
#> 1     ALD   city   Alder     alias                         <NA>
#> 2   grove   city   Grove     exact                         <NA>
#> 3     HBR region Harbour     alias                         <NA>
#> 4 Harbour   <NA>    <NA> ambiguous region/Harbour; city/Harbour
#> 5     Zed   <NA>    <NA>      none                         <NA>
scale_match(places, "Harbour", frame = "city")
#>     label frame  member method candidates
#> 1 Harbour  city Harbour  exact       <NA>

Attaching the hierarchy, and colours

A table keyed by city gets its region and country with one join; the added columns are prefixed by the scale’s name, so a second scale on the same table never collides with the first.

join_scale(pop[c("city", "people_k")], places, frame = "city",
           attach = TRUE)
#>    city people_k places.country places.region places
#> 1 Alder        3          North            N1  Alder
#> 2 Cedar        5          North            N2  Cedar
#> 3   Elm        6          South            S1    Elm
#> 4 Grove        7          South            S1  Grove

Colours are presentation and are not stored on a scale. When a figure needs them, they are joined by member name from the palette it uses – the article Fuels, regions and months on the package site does so.

Values that differ by year

The values above have no date. A household size counted in one year and again ten years later is the same attribute of the same city with a different year – a second dimension, not a deeper frame. That belongs to a scale_product() of the scale of places and a scale of years, such as a Calendar from timescales, with the values of each year attached as their own source; it is not built in this version.
